stem: Which enzyme digests starch?

options.content: Lipase
options.rationale: Lipase digests fats and oils.

options.content: Amylase
options.rationale: Amylase breaks starch down into maltose.

options.content: Protease
options.rationale: Proteases digest proteins.

options.content: Rennin
options.rationale: Rennin clots milk protein.

explanation: Amylase, made by the salivary glands and the pancreas, breaks starch down into the sugar maltose.
hints: The name of the enzyme comes from the Latin word for starch, 'amylum'.

stem: What are the products of fat digestion by lipase?

options.content: Glycerol and amino acids
options.rationale: Glycerol is one product, but amino acids come from protein digestion, not fat digestion.

options.content: Maltose
options.rationale: Maltose is produced from starch by amylase.

options.content: Fatty acids only
options.rationale: There is a second product as well.

options.content: Fatty acids and glycerol
options.rationale: Lipase breaks each fat molecule into fatty acids and glycerol.

explanation: Lipase digests fats and oils into fatty acids and glycerol, which are small enough to be absorbed in the small intestine.
hints: There are two products.

stem: True or false: the hydrochloric acid in the stomach digests proteins into amino acids.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not true. Proteases digest protein; the acid kills microorganisms and gives the protease its optimum pH.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct. The acid does not digest food: it kills microorganisms and provides the acidic pH that the stomach protease needs.

explanation: Proteins are digested by proteases. Hydrochloric acid kills many microorganisms in food and makes the stomach acidic, which is the optimum pH for the stomach protease (pepsin).
hints: Which kind of substance digests protein?

stem: Which statement describes the functions of hydrochloric acid in gastric juice?

options.content: It kills microorganisms and gives the acid pH the stomach protease needs.
options.rationale: These are the two functions of the acid.

options.content: It digests starch and kills harmful microorganisms.
options.rationale: Starch is digested by amylase, and amylase does not work in strong acid.

options.content: It neutralises bile and emulsifies fat.
options.rationale: Bile neutralises acid; the acid does not emulsify fat.

options.content: It breaks proteins into amino acids and fats into fatty acids and glycerol.
options.rationale: Enzymes do this, not the acid.

explanation: Hydrochloric acid kills many harmful microorganisms in food and drink, and it makes the stomach contents acidic (about pH 2), which is the optimum pH for pepsin.
hints: The acid has a protective role and helps an enzyme.

stem: Match each enzyme with the product(s) of its reaction.
explanation: Amylase: starch → maltose. Protease: protein → amino acids. Lipase: fats → fatty acids and glycerol. Starch and proteins are substrates, not products.
hints: Two of the options are substrates, not products.

stem: Name the organ that makes the lipase that digests fats in the small intestine.

rejected.feedback: The liver makes bile, which contains no enzymes.
The gall bladder stores bile, which contains no enzymes.
The stomach makes a protease, not the lipase that acts in the small intestine.

explanation: The pancreas makes pancreatic juice, which contains lipase (as well as amylase and protease) and flows into the duodenum.
hints: It also makes amylase and protease and releases them into the duodenum.

stem: Where do the enzymes in pancreatic juice digest food?

options.content: In the mouth
options.rationale: Only salivary amylase works in the mouth.

options.content: In the stomach
options.rationale: Pancreatic juice does not enter the stomach.

options.content: In the small intestine
options.rationale: Pancreatic juice enters the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine.

options.content: In the pancreas itself
options.rationale: The enzymes are made in the pancreas but act in the gut.

explanation: Pancreatic juice flows along the pancreatic duct into the duodenum. Its amylase, protease and lipase digest food in the small intestine.
hints: Where does the pancreatic duct open?

stem: Complete the sentences about protein digestion.

payload.template: In the acidic conditions of the stomach, protein is digested by the protease {{blank:pep}}. In the alkaline conditions of the small intestine, protein is digested by the protease {{blank:try}}, which is made in the {{blank:pan}}.

explanation: Pepsin, made by the stomach, works at about pH 2. Trypsin, made by the pancreas, works in the alkaline conditions of the small intestine. Both break proteins down towards amino acids.
hints: The stomach protease starts with 'pep'.

stem: Where does maltase act to break maltose down into glucose?

options.content: In the mouth, after being released in saliva
options.rationale: Saliva contains amylase, which makes maltose but does not break it down.

options.content: In the stomach, after being released in gastric juice
options.rationale: Gastric juice contains a protease, not maltase.

options.content: In the duodenum, after being released in pancreatic juice
options.rationale: Pancreatic juice contains amylase, protease and lipase.

options.content: On the membranes of the cells lining the small intestine
options.rationale: Maltase stays on the epithelium, so glucose is made where it is absorbed.

explanation: Maltase is held on the membranes of the epithelial cells lining the small intestine. Maltose made by amylase is broken into glucose right at the surface where glucose is absorbed.
hints: Maltase is not released into the gut contents at all.

stem: Why is the alkaline nature of bile important for digestion in the small intestine?

options.content: It provides lipase enzymes that digest fat into fatty acids and glycerol.
options.rationale: Bile contains no enzymes; lipase comes from the pancreas.

options.content: It neutralises stomach acid, giving a good pH for intestinal enzymes.
options.rationale: Pancreatic and intestinal enzymes work best in slightly alkaline conditions.

options.content: It kills the bacteria that enter the small intestine with the food.
options.rationale: Killing microorganisms is a job of stomach acid.

options.content: It turns starch into maltose in the small intestine.
options.rationale: That is the job of amylase.

explanation: The food leaving the stomach is acidic. Bile is alkaline and neutralises it, so the pH in the small intestine suits enzymes such as pancreatic amylase, trypsin and lipase.
hints: The food arriving from the stomach is acidic.

stem: Salivary amylase digests starch in the mouth, but it stops working once the food reaches the stomach. What is the best explanation?

options.content: All the starch has already been digested in the mouth.
options.rationale: Food stays in the mouth for a short time, so only a little starch is digested there.

options.content: The stomach is too warm for amylase.
options.rationale: The stomach is at body temperature, close to amylase's optimum.

options.content: The stomach is strongly acidic, so amylase's active site changes shape.
options.rationale: Amylase works best at about pH 7; acid changes its shape and stops it.

options.content: The amylase is digested by bile as soon as it reaches the stomach contents.
options.rationale: Bile enters the duodenum, not the stomach, and contains no enzymes.

explanation: Salivary amylase has an optimum pH of about 7. The hydrochloric acid in the stomach (about pH 2) changes the shape of its active site, so starch no longer fits and digestion stops until pancreatic amylase acts in the duodenum.
hints: Think about the pH in the stomach and the optimum pH of salivary amylase.

stem: What is the function of rennin?

options.content: It clots milk protein in the stomach.
options.rationale: Clotted milk stays in the stomach longer, so proteases have more time to digest it.

options.content: It digests starch in the mouth.
options.rationale: That is the job of salivary amylase.

options.content: It emulsifies fats in the duodenum.
options.rationale: Bile emulsifies fats; it is not an enzyme.

options.content: It breaks maltose down into glucose.
options.rationale: That is the job of maltase.

explanation: Rennin, made by the stomach, clots (coagulates) the soluble protein in milk. The semi-solid curd stays in the stomach longer, so proteases have more time to digest it.
hints: Rennin is also used to make cheese from milk.

stem: True or false: rennin is mainly important in young mammals, such as calves, whose diet is milk.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct. Rennin clots milk protein, so it matters most to young mammals that feed only on milk.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true. Rennin clots milk protein, so it is most important in young mammals that feed on milk.

explanation: Rennin clots the protein in milk so it stays in the stomach long enough to be digested. This matters most in young mammals, such as calves, that live on milk.
hints: Which food does rennin act on?

stem: A Visking tubing bag containing starch solution and amylase was left in a beaker of water at 37 °C for 30 minutes. The water outside the bag was then tested. Which results are expected?

options.content: Iodine test: blue-black. Benedict's test: brick-red.
options.rationale: Starch molecules are too large to pass through the tubing, so the iodine test outside stays orange-brown.

options.content: Iodine test: orange-brown. Benedict's test: brick-red.
options.rationale: Maltose passed out of the bag; starch did not.

options.content: Iodine test: blue-black. Benedict's test: blue.
options.rationale: This would mean starch passed out and no sugar was made: both are wrong.

options.content: Iodine test: orange-brown. Benedict's test: blue.
options.rationale: Amylase made maltose, which is small enough to pass through the tubing.

explanation: Amylase digested the starch into maltose. Maltose molecules are small enough to pass through the partially permeable tubing, so the water outside gives a brick-red Benedict's result. Starch molecules are too large to pass through, so the iodine stays orange-brown.
hints: Which molecules are small enough to pass through Visking tubing?

stem:
Tendai placed cubes of boiled egg white, each with a mass of 1.00 g, in tubes of pepsin solution buffered at different pH values. The tubes were kept at 37 °C for 24 hours and then the cubes were blotted dry and weighed.

| pH | 1 | 2 | 4 | 7 | 9 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mass of cube remaining / g | 0.35 | 0.20 | 0.62 | 0.98 | 1.00 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage of the egg white that was digested at pH 2.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which pH was the best of those tested for pepsin?

options.content: pH 2
options.rationale: The least mass remained, so the most protein was digested.

options.content: pH 1
options.rationale: Less protein was digested at pH 1 than at pH 2.

options.content: pH 7
options.rationale: Almost nothing was digested at pH 7.

options.content: pH 9
options.rationale: Nothing was digested at pH 9.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why almost no egg white was digested at pH 7 and pH 9.

points.description: pH 7 and 9 are far from pepsin's optimum (about pH 2) / pepsin needs acid
The shape of the active site changes (pepsin denatured), so protein no longer fits / no enzyme-substrate complexes form

parts.explanation: Pepsin works in acid, with an optimum near pH 2. At pH 7 and 9 the shape of its active site is changed, so the protein substrate no longer fits and almost none is digested.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Describe a suitable control for this investigation.

points.description: A cube of egg white in boiled (denatured) pepsin at pH 2 / in buffer at pH 2 without pepsin, kept at 37 °C

parts.explanation: A cube of egg white in boiled pepsin solution (or buffer with no pepsin) at pH 2 and 37 °C, to show that the loss of mass is caused by the enzyme.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Use the results to explain why hydrochloric acid in the stomach is important for protein digestion.

points.description: The acid keeps the stomach at a low pH (about 2)
which is the optimum pH for pepsin, so protein is digested fastest / the acid itself does not digest protein

parts.explanation: Hydrochloric acid keeps the stomach at about pH 2, the optimum pH for pepsin shown by these results, so protein is digested quickly. The acid itself does not digest the protein.

explanation: At pH 2, $1.00 - 0.20 = 0.80$ g was digested, which is $\dfrac{0.80}{1.00} \times 100 = 80\%$. The most digestion happened at pH 2, close to the pH of the stomach, because hydrochloric acid provides the optimum pH for pepsin. Far from the optimum the active site changes shape and little or no protein is digested.
hints: The less mass that remains, the more protein was digested.
Pepsin comes from the stomach: what is the pH there?

stem: Complete the information about digestive enzymes.

payload.template: Amylase is made in the salivary glands and the {{blank:organ}}. Its substrate is {{blank:sub}} and its product is {{blank:prod}}.
Protease breaks protein down into {{blank:aa}}. One place where protease acts is the {{blank:place}}.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Lipase acts in the small intestine. Name the products of its reaction.

accepted.value: three fatty acids and one glycerol

rejected.feedback: Give both products: fatty acids and glycerol.
Give both products: fatty acids and glycerol.
Amino acids come from protein digestion.

explanation: Amylase (salivary glands and pancreas): starch → maltose. Protease (stomach, pancreas and small intestine): protein → amino acids. Lipase (pancreas, acting in the small intestine): fats → fatty acids and glycerol.
hints: For (c), there are two products.

stem: Describe how starch in a meal of sadza is digested to glucose. Name the enzymes, where they are made and where they act. [5]

points.description: Salivary amylase (from the salivary glands) begins digesting starch to maltose in the mouth
Amylase stops working in the stomach because of the acid (low pH)
Pancreatic amylase (from the pancreas) continues digesting starch to maltose in the duodenum / small intestine
Bile neutralises the stomach acid, giving a suitable pH for amylase
Maltase breaks maltose down to glucose
Maltase is on the membranes of the epithelium lining the small intestine

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Starch digestion begins in the mouth, where amylase in saliva from the salivary glands breaks some starch down into maltose. In the stomach the acid changes the shape of amylase, so starch digestion stops. In the duodenum, bile neutralises the acid and pancreatic amylase, made by the pancreas, digests the rest of the starch to maltose. Finally maltase, which is held on the membranes of the epithelial cells lining the small intestine, breaks maltose down into glucose, which is absorbed into the blood.

explanation: Starch → maltose by amylase (mouth, then small intestine); maltose → glucose by maltase on the intestinal lining. Acid in the stomach stops salivary amylase; bile makes the pH suitable again.
hints: Two enzymes are needed: one makes maltose, the other glucose.
Follow the food from the mouth to the small intestine.

stem: Why must starch, proteins and fats be digested before the body can use them?

options.content: They are poisonous until they are digested.
options.rationale: They are not poisonous; they are simply too large to be absorbed.

options.content: Enzymes add energy to them during digestion.
options.rationale: Digestion does not add energy to food.

options.content: They must be turned into water before they can enter the blood.
options.rationale: They are turned into small soluble molecules, not water.

options.content: Their molecules are too large and insoluble to pass into the blood.
options.rationale: Digestion produces small soluble molecules that can be absorbed.

explanation: Starch, proteins and fats are large, insoluble molecules that cannot pass through the lining of the small intestine. Enzymes break them into small, soluble molecules (sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol) that can be absorbed.
hints: Think about the size of the molecules and the wall of the gut.

stem: Name the small, soluble molecules produced when proteins are completely digested.

rejected.feedback: Peptides are short chains; complete digestion gives amino acids.

explanation: Proteases break proteins down into amino acids, which are absorbed in the small intestine and used by cells to build new proteins.
hints: They are the building blocks of proteins.

stem: In some people the duct from the pancreas becomes blocked, so pancreatic juice cannot reach the duodenum. Bile still reaches the duodenum normally.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which enzymes no longer reach the duodenum?

options.content: Pepsin, maltase and rennin
options.rationale: None of these is made by the pancreas.

options.content: Salivary amylase and pepsin
options.rationale: These are made by the salivary glands and the stomach.

options.content: Amylase, protease and lipase
options.rationale: These are the enzymes of pancreatic juice.

options.content: Bile and lipase
options.rationale: Bile still arrives, and bile is not an enzyme.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Suggest why these people produce faeces that contain a lot of fat.

points.description: Lipase (made only by the pancreas) cannot reach the food, so fat is not digested into fatty acids and glycerol
Undigested fat cannot be absorbed, so it passes into the faeces

parts.explanation: Lipase comes from the pancreas, so very little fat is digested to fatty acids and glycerol. Undigested fat molecules are too large to be absorbed, so the fat passes out in the faeces.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Suggest why some starch is still digested in these people.

points.description: Salivary amylase digests some starch in the mouth
Maltase on the intestinal lining is still present / some maltose made in the mouth can still be turned into glucose

parts.explanation: Amylase in saliva still digests some starch to maltose in the mouth, and maltase on the lining of the small intestine (which does not come from the pancreas) can still turn maltose into glucose.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Doctors give these people capsules containing pancreatic enzymes to swallow with every meal. Explain why this helps, and why the capsules are designed so that they release their enzymes in the small intestine rather than in the stomach.

points.description: The capsules supply the missing enzymes so fat, protein and starch can be digested and absorbed
In the stomach the acid would denature the enzymes / change the shape of their active sites (they work in alkaline conditions)

parts.explanation: The capsules replace the missing pancreatic enzymes, so food can be digested and absorbed again. If they released the enzymes in the stomach, the acid would change the shape of their active sites; released in the small intestine, where bile has neutralised the acid, they work at a suitable pH.

explanation: Pancreatic juice carries amylase, protease and lipase. Without it, little fat is digested (fatty faeces) and protein and starch digestion are reduced, although salivary amylase and the enzymes on the intestinal lining still work. Enzyme capsules replace the missing enzymes, and releasing them after the stomach protects them from acid.
hints: List the enzymes in pancreatic juice.
Which enzymes are made somewhere other than the pancreas?

stem: True or false: bile contains enzymes that digest fat.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not true. Bile contains no enzymes; lipase from the pancreas digests fat.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct. Bile contains no enzymes. It emulsifies fat, and lipase digests it.

explanation: Bile is made in the liver and contains no enzymes. It emulsifies fats and neutralises stomach acid. Fat is digested by lipase from the pancreas.
hints: Where does lipase come from?

stem:
A cloudy suspension of milk protein goes clear when the protein is digested. A student added two proteases to the suspension at two different pH values and timed how long each tube took to go clear at 37 °C.

| Tube | Enzyme | pH | Time to go clear / min |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | Pepsin | 2 | 4 |
| B | Pepsin | 8 | no change after 30 |
| C | Trypsin | 2 | no change after 30 |
| D | Trypsin | 8 | 5 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which conclusion is supported by the results?

options.content: Pepsin works in acid conditions and trypsin in alkaline ones.
options.rationale: Each enzyme worked at only one of the two pH values.

options.content: Both enzymes work best in acid.
options.rationale: Trypsin did not work at pH 2.

options.content: Neither enzyme is affected by the pH at all.
options.rationale: Each enzyme failed at one pH value.

options.content: Trypsin works faster than pepsin at every one of the pH values tested.
options.rationale: Trypsin did nothing at pH 2.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Rate = 100 ÷ time. Calculate the rate for tube A.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why pepsin did not digest the protein at pH 8.

points.description: pH 8 is far from pepsin's optimum (about pH 2)
so its active site changes shape / it is denatured, and the protein no longer fits

parts.explanation: Pepsin's optimum pH is about 2. At pH 8 the shape of its active site changes, so the protein substrate no longer fits and no digestion happens.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Relate the results to the places in the gut where pepsin and trypsin work.

points.description: Pepsin works in the stomach, where hydrochloric acid makes the contents acidic
Trypsin works in the small intestine, where bile has neutralised the acid / conditions are alkaline

parts.explanation: Pepsin acts in the stomach, which hydrochloric acid keeps at about pH 2. Trypsin, from the pancreas, acts in the small intestine, where alkaline bile has neutralised the acid from the stomach.

explanation: Pepsin cleared the suspension only at pH 2 and trypsin only at pH 8: each works at the pH of the part of the gut where it acts. Rate for A $= \dfrac{100}{4} = 25$ per minute. Far from the optimum pH, the active site changes shape so the protein no longer fits.
hints: Compare each enzyme at the two pH values.
Which part of the gut is acidic, and which is alkaline?
